Q. At a fish market, today’s fish sells for $10, but next week’s promised fish sells for $12. Traders who must renew their position every week end up selling at $10 and buying again at $12, slowly losing money - economists call this situation X. In other years the opposite happens: today’s fish sells for $12, while next week’s promise sells for $10, so traders sell high and buy cheaper, gaining a little each time they renew - economists call this Y.
These two conditions famously showed up in oil markets during the 2020 oil futures negative price event when specifically storage shortages pushed the market heavily into X, hurting funds like United States Oil Fund (USO). What are X and Y?
